# Google's New Android Sideloading Restrictions: 24-Hour Lock Implemented

Google is implementing significant changes to Android's sideloading process, introducing a mandatory 24-hour waiting period for installing apps from unverified developers. The new "advanced flow" requires users to enable developer mode, confirm they're not being coerced, restart their phone, wait a full day, and then re-authenticate using biometrics or a PIN. Google designed this deliberately tedious process to combat scams and coercion tactics, giving users time to reconsider potentially harmful installations. While sideloading remains possible, the added friction and verification requirements have sparked concerns about Android's openness. The company aims to protect users from malicious apps and social engineering attacks while maintaining access for advanced users who genuinely need to install apps outside the Play Store.
highlights.content:
TL;DR

- Google is introducing a new sideloading flow on Android that includes a mandatory 24-hour lock and multiple steps when installing apps from unverified developers.

- The change is aimed at preventing scams and coercion, forcing users to slow down and think before installing potentially harmful apps.

- While sideloading is still possible, the added friction and new developer verification requirements could raise concerns that Android is becoming less open.

When Google execs previously [said](https://www.androidauthority.com/google-sideloading-android-high-friction-process-3633468/) sideloading would become a high-friction process on Android, they really weren’t kidding.

The company is finally sharing what Android’s new sideloading flow will look like in practice, and if you’re someone who installs apps outside the Play Store, you’re going to feel it immediately, and you’re going to feel it deeply.

This isn’t a subtle tweak or another warning screen you can quickly tap past. Google is fundamentally changing how sideloading works on Android for apps that come from unverified developers.

Google’s brand-new “advanced flow” for sideloading is designed specifically for what the company calls power users. It’s a deliberately slow and almost impossible-to-rush-through process that will allow advanced Android users to sideload apps from unverified developers, while giving them plenty of caution to keep them safe from malicious apps and bad actors. At the same time, the new process is designed to protect unassuming Android users who might be tricked or coerced into downloading unverified apps.

## The new sideloading flow: what you actually have to do

![](https://www.androidauthority.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/android-developer-verifirication-sideload-3.jpg)When Android’s new sideloading rules come into force, installing apps from developers without Google verification (more on that later) will become extremely tedious by design and **require a 24-hour lock before users can install them**. Here’s what the new flow will look like:

- **Step 1: Enable Developer Mode**

No more quick toggles. You’ll need to manually [enable developer options](https://www.androidauthority.com/enable-developer-options-569223/) first, adding an intentional layer of friction.

- **Step 2: Confirm you’re not being coerced**

Android will explicitly ask if someone is guiding you through disabling protections on your device as a direct response to scam tactics.

- **Step 3: Restart your phone**

This cuts off active calls, remote access, or screen-sharing sessions, which scammers often rely on.

- **Step 4: Wait 24 hours**

Yes, really. There’s a mandatory one-time, one-day waiting period before you can proceed and sideload an app from an unverified developer. Google calls it a “protective waiting period.”

- **Step 5: Re-authenticate**

After the one-day wait, you’ll need biometric authentication or your PIN to confirm it’s really you. “Scammers rely on manufactured urgency, so this breaks their spell and gives you time to think,” Google notes in its blog.

- **Step 6: Finally, install the app**

Only then can you sideload, with the option to allow installs for seven days or indefinitely. Even within that seven-day time frame, once sideloading is enabled you can install as many different APKs from as many different unverified developers as you like.

Even after all this, Android will still show a warning that the app is from an unverified developer, but at that point, you can tap “Install anyway.”

### What do you think about Android's new sideloading flow for unverified apps?

1236 votes

Essentially, Google is making sure that sideloading apps from unverified sources is no longer something you can do on impulse.

## Why is Google doing this?

![](https://www.androidauthority.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Google-Play-Protect-Apps-scanned-scaled.jpg)Aamir Siddiqui / Android Authority

Google’s reasoning is pretty clear, and something the company has been saying for a long time now. Android today isn’t the scrappy, enthusiast platform it once was, it’s the primary computing device for billions of people.

Speaking about the new rules in an interview with *Android Authority*, Google’s President of the Android Ecosystem, Sameer Samat, said,

“You want a platform to be open, but you need a platform to be safe.”

In Google’s view, safety is increasingly at odds with how sideloading has traditionally worked. Attackers frequently use social engineering and panic-inducing phone calls about legal trouble or a family emergency to walk victims through disabling protections and installing malicious apps.

The problem isn’t that Android’s warnings don’t work. It’s that they are insufficient, and in high-pressure situations, people often ignore them. Google says the new system is designed to break that cycle.

Google acknowledges that the 24-hour wait isn't just about stopping scams, it's also about what users will tolerate.

The restart step will cut off scammers watching or guiding victims through installations. The 24-hour delay will kill the urgency that scams depend on, and the extra confirmation will give users time to pause and consider their actions.

Internally, Google even acknowledged that the 24-hour wait isn’t just about stopping scams, it’s also about what users will tolerate. Google told us that they worked with power users to land on a delay that’s annoying, but not deal-breaking.

## What does Google mean by apps from unverified developers?

![](https://www.androidauthority.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Photo-of-Android-Developer-Verifier-app-on-an-Android-phone-scaled.jpg)Mishaal Rahman / Android Authority

The new sideloading flow is part of Google’s broader push that will require Android app developers to [verify their identity](https://www.androidauthority.com/how-android-app-verification-works-3603559/) with the company. Google wants to tie apps to verified developers in hopes of reducing the number of bad actors slipping through the cracks.

“We would like to be able to tell the user this app is from this source. Now, that doesn’t mean that the app is safe. The user still has to make decisions. But at least you know who it’s from, and you can decide better — Do I trust this person, or do I not? That’s very important,” Samat previously told *Android Authority* in [a recent interview](https://www.androidauthority.com/google-android-17-sideloading-interview-sameer-samat-3647478/).

There are some exceptions to Google’s developer verification rules, though.

Limited distribution apps, such as student or hobby projects, can still be shared with up to 20 devices without full verification.

## When will the new sideloading rules come into effect, and what does this mean for you?

![](https://www.androidauthority.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/Send-Files-To-TV-app-for-Sideloading-apps-on-Android-TV-scaled.jpg)Adamya Sharma / Android Authority

According to Google, “Limited distribution accounts and advanced flow for users will be available in August before the new developer verification requirements take effect.”

The new advanced sideloading flow for users will be available in August.

The company said it will be sharing more details and technical documentation regarding these updates in the coming days and weeks.

Executives emphasized to us that this rollout has always been meant to evolve with feedback and that the company is listening. Still, for [developers who rely on sideloading or alternative distribution](https://www.androidauthority.com/google-android-sideloading-claims-misleading-f-droid-3611139/), this marks a significant shift in how open Android really feels.

For everyday users, nothing changes as long as you stick to the Play Store. But if you use third-party app stores or install APKs manually, you’re now in for a much more restrictive process.

It remains to be seen how the developer community reacts to these changes and if they will encourage developers to sign up for Google’s new verification system. If your favorite developer decides to remain unverified, you’re going to have to go through the new process for any app you install from them.

highlights.title: Consensus Board Game
highlights.summary:
<think>The user wants me to summarize this article about the consensus board game in 100-200 words. Let me analyze the content:

The article is about explaining consensus algorithms through a visual "board game" metaphor. Key points:

1. The author has trauma from struggling to understand consensus and is overcompensating by creating clearer explanations
2. This is meant to complement "Notes on Paxos" - this is the visual/mathematical counterpart
3. The core concept is explaining consensus through a committee voting analogy
4. The setup: 5 committee members trying to choose a color for a bike shed
5. The fundamental idea is simple majority vote (3 out of 5)
6. The problem: voting can get stuck (shown in diagrams)
7. The author is focusing on the mathematics/logic of consensus, not practical engineering

I need to summarize this concisely in 100-200 words, focusing on key points and main takeaways.
</think>

# Summary: Consensus Board Game

This article uses a visual "board game" metaphor to explain consensus algorithms. The author, motivated by past struggles understanding consensus, presents illustrations to clarify the concept as a complement to more formal explanations.

The core analogy involves five committee members (R0-R4) trying to decide on a bike shed color. Consensus relies on simple majority voting—three out of five votes determines the outcome. The author demonstrates this through board diagrams showing successful votes and potential deadlocks.

The article focuses strictly on the mathematical foundations of consensus: what makes certain outcomes possible or impossible in distributed systems. While acknowledging this is just one piece of the broader engineering puzzle, the visual approach aims to make the logical structure behind consensus algorithms more accessible.
highlights.content:
Mar 19, 2026
        
        
          I have an early adulthood trauma from struggling to understand
          consensus amidst a myriad of poor explanations. I am overcompensating
          for that by adding my own attempts to the fray. Today, I want to draw
          a series of pictures which could be helpful. You can see this post as
          a set of missing illustrations for
          [*Notes on Paxos*](https://matklad.github.io/2020/11/01/notes-on-paxos.html), or, alternatively, you can view *that* post as a more formal narrative counter-part for the
          present one.
        

        
          The idea comes from my [mathematics of consensus](https://tigerbeetle.com/blog/2025-11-22-mathematics-of-consensus/)
          lecture, with versions in [English](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=thY12Wnrmyw) and
          [Russian](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=h8nj65jvXl0).
        

        
          
## [The Preamble](#The-Preamble)

          
            I am going to *aggressively* hand wave the details away,
            please refer to
            [*Notes*](https://matklad.github.io/2020/11/01/notes-on-paxos.html) for filling in the blanks.
          

          
            And, before we begin, I want to stress again that here I am focusing
            strictly on the *mathematics*
            behind the algorithm, on the logical structure of the universe that
            makes some things impossible, and others doable. Consensus is but a
            small part of the engineering behind real data management systems,
            and I might do something about *pragmatics* of consensus at
            some point, just not today ;)
          

        
        
          
## [The Problem](#The-Problem)

          
            There’s a committee of five members that tries to choose a color for
            a bike shed, but the committee members are not entirely reliable. We
            want to arrive at a decision even if some members of the committee
            are absent.
          

        
        
          
## [The Vote](#The-Vote)

          
            The fundamental idea underpinning consensus is simple majority vote.
            If R0, … R4 are the five committee members, we can use the following
            board to record the votes:
          

          
            ![](https://matklad.github.io/assets/2026-03-19-consensus-board-game/blank.svg)
          
          A successful vote looks like this:

          
            ![](https://matklad.github.io/assets/2026-03-19-consensus-board-game/red-wins.svg)
          
          
            Here, red collected 3 out of 5 votes and wins. Note that R4 hasn’t
            voted yet. It might, or might not do so eventually, but that won’t
            affect the outcome.
          

          The problem with voting is that it can get stuck like this:

          
            ![](https://matklad.github.io/assets/2026-03-19-consensus-board-game/stuck.svg)
          
          
            Here, we have two votes for red, two votes for blue, but the
            potential tie-breaker, R4, voted for green, the rascal!
          

          
            To solve split vote, we are going to designate R0 as the committee’s
            leader, make it choose the color, and allow others only to approve.
            Note that meaningful voting still takes place, as someone might
            abstain from voting — you need at least 50% turnout for the vote to
            be complete:
          

          
            ![](https://matklad.github.io/assets/2026-03-19-consensus-board-game/leader.svg)
          
          
            Here, R0, the leader (marked with yellow napoleonic bicorne), choose
            red, R2 and R3 acquiesced, so the red “won”, even as R1 and R4
            abstained (x signifies absence of a vote).
          

          
            The problem with *this* is that our designated leader might
            be unavailable itself:
          

          
            ![](https://matklad.github.io/assets/2026-03-19-consensus-board-game/leader-dead.svg)
          
        
        
          
## [The Board](#The-Board)

          
            Which brings us to the central illustration that I wanted to share.
            What are we going to do now is to *multiply* our voting.
            Instead of conducting just one vote with a designated leader, the
            committee will conduct a series of concurrent votes, where the
            leaders rotate in round-robin pattern. This gives rise to the
            following half-infinite 2D board on which the game of consensus is
            played:
          

          
            ![](https://matklad.github.io/assets/2026-03-19-consensus-board-game/board-blank.svg)
          
          
            Each column plays independently. If you are a leader in a column,
            and your cell is blank, you can choose whatever color. If you are a
            follower, you need to wait until column’s leader decision, and then
            you can either fill the same color, or you can abstain. After
            several rounds the board might end up looking like this:
          

          
            ![](https://matklad.github.io/assets/2026-03-19-consensus-board-game/board-filled.svg)
          
          
            The benefit of our 2D setup is that, if any committee member is
            unavailable, *their* columns might get stuck, but, as long as
            the majority is available, some column somewhere might still
            complete. The drawback is that, while individual column’s decision
            is clear and unambiguous, the outcome of the board as whole is
            undefined. In the above example, there’s a column where red wins,
            and a column where blue wins.
          

          
            So what we are going to do is to scrap the above board as invalid,
            and instead *require* that any two columns that achieved
            majorities *must* agree on the color. In other words, the
            outcome of the entire board is the outcome of any of its columns,
            whichever finishes first, and the safety condition is that no two
            colors can reach majorities in different columns.
          

          
            Let’s take a few steps back when the board wasn’t yet hosed, and try
            to think about the choice of the next move from the perspective of
            R3:
          

          
            ![](https://matklad.github.io/assets/2026-03-19-consensus-board-game/board-choice.svg)
          
          
            As R3 and the leader for your column, you need to pick a color which
            won’t conflict with any past or *future* decisions in other
            columns. Given that there are some greens and blues already, it
            *feels* like maybe you shouldn’t pick red… But it could be
            the case that the three partially filled columns won’t move anywhere
            in the future, and the first column gets a solid red line! Though
            choices! You need to worry about the future *and* the
            infinite number of columns to your right!
          

          
            Luckily, the problem can be made much easier if we assume that
            everyone plays by the same rules, in which case it’s enough to only
            worry about the columns to your left. Suppose that you, and everyone
            else is carefully choosing their moves to not conflict with the
            columns to the left. Then, if you chose red, your column wins, and
            subsequently some buffoon on the right chooses green, it’s *their*
            problem, because you are to their left.
          

          
            So let’s just focus on the left part of the board. Again, it seems
            like blue or green might be good bets, as they are already present
            on the board, but there’s a chance that the first column will
            eventually vote for red. To prevent that, what we are going to do is
            to collect a majority of participants (R0, R2, R3) and require them
            to commit to *not* voting in the first columns. Actually, for
            that matter, let’s prevent them from voting in *any* column
            to the left:
          

          
            ![](https://matklad.github.io/assets/2026-03-19-consensus-board-game/board-x.svg)
          
          
            Here, you asked R0, R2 and R3 to abstain from casting further votes
            in the first three columns, signified by black x. With this picture,
            we can now be sure that red can not win in the first column — no
            color can win there, because only two out of the five votes are
            available there!
          

          
            Still, we have the choice between green and blue, which one should
            we pick? The answer is the rightmost. R2, the participant that
            picked blue in the column to our immediate left, was executing the
            same algorithm. If they picked blue, they did it because they knew
            for certain that the second column can’t eventually vote for green.
            R2 got a different majority of participants to abstain from voting
            in the second column, and, while we, as R3, don’t know which
            majority that was, we know that it exists because we know that R2
            did pick blue, and we assume fair play.
          

          
          
            That’s all for today, that’s the trick that makes consensus click,
            in the abstract. In a full distributed system the situation is more
            complicated. Each participant only sees its own row, the board as a
            whole remains concealed. Participants can learn something about
            others’ state by communicating, but the knowledge isn’t strongly
            anchored at time. By the time a response is received the answer
            could as well be obsolete. And yet, the above birds-eye view can be
            implemented in a few exchanges of messages.
          

          
            Please see the
            [*Notes*](https://matklad.github.io/2020/11/01/notes-on-paxos.html)
            for further details.

highlights.title: Google Search Is Now Using AI to Rewrite Headlines
highlights.summary: Google has begun using AI to rewrite headlines in its traditional search results, expanding a practice previously limited to its Google Discover news feed. The company confirmed this is currently a "small" and "narrow" experiment, though it wouldn't specify the scope. The Verge has documented multiple instances where their original headlines were replaced with AI-generated versions that sometimes altered the meaning—for example, reducing a headline about an AI tool that doesn't help with cheating to just "'Cheat on everything' AI tool," which could imply endorsement of a product they don't recommend. Google isn't applying this only to news sites, but to how all websites appear in search results. The article compares this to "a bookstore ripping the covers off the books it puts on display and changing their titles," arguing publishers have a right to present their own work. While these changes remain relatively rare in traditional search, they represent a troubling expansion of AI-generated content that replaces editorial choices without clear disclosure.
highlights.content:
Since roughly the turn of the millennium, Google Search has been the bedrock of the web. People loved Google’s trustworthy “10 blue links” search experience and its unspoken promise: The website you click is the website you get.

Now, Google is beginning to replace news headlines in its search results with ones that are AI-generated. After doing something similar [in its Google Discover news feed](https://www.theverge.com/tech/865168/google-says-ai-news-headlines-are-feature-not-experiment), it’s starting to mess with headlines in the traditional “10 blue links,” too. We’ve found multiple examples where Google replaced headlines we wrote with ones we did not, sometimes changing their meaning in the process.

For example, Google reduced our headline “[I used the ‘cheat on everything’ AI tool and it didn’t help me cheat on anything](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/654223/cheat-on-everything-ai)” to just five words: “‘Cheat on everything’ AI tool.” It *almost* sounds like we’re endorsing a product we do not recommend at all.

What we are seeing is a “small” and “narrow” experiment, one that’s not yet approved for a fuller launch, Google spokespeople Jennifer Kutz, Mallory De Leon, and Ned Adriance tell *The Verge*. They would not say how “small” that experiment actually is. Over the past few months, multiple *Verge* staffers have seen examples of headlines that we never wrote appear in Google Search results — headlines that do not follow our editorial style, and without any indication that Google replaced the words we chose. And Google says it’s tweaking how other websites show up in search, too, not just news.

Like I wrote in January, when Google decided it [wouldn’t stop replacing news headlines in Google Discover](https://www.theverge.com/tech/865168/google-says-ai-news-headlines-are-feature-not-experiment) from *The Verge* and our competitors, this is like a bookstore ripping the covers off the books it puts on display and changing their titles. We spend a lot of time trying to write headlines that are true, interesting, fun, and worthy of your attention without resorting to clickbait, but Google seems to believe we don’t have an inherent right to market our own work that way.

*(Disclosure: Vox Media, The Verge’s parent company, has [filed a lawsuit against Google](https://www.theverge.com/news/861897/atlantic-penske-vox-google-ad-tech-antitrust-lawsuits), seeking damages from its illegal ad tech monopoly.)*

The good news, for now, is that these changed headlines seem to be few and far between, and they’re not yet the kind of tripe we’ve seen in Google Discover. (For example, Google Discover told me this week that the PlayStation Portal was getting a 1080p streaming mode, when it actually got [a *higher bitrate* mode](https://www.theverge.com/games/896282/the-playstation-portals-new-software-update-adds-higher-bitrate-1080p-streaming#comments) instead.)

Compared to that and [other lying Google Discover headlines](https://www.theverge.com/tech/865168/google-says-ai-news-headlines-are-feature-not-experiment#:~:text=%E2%80%9CUS%20reverses%20foreign%20drone%20ban%2C) like “US reverses foreign drone ban” — on a story reporting the opposite** — **the nonsense headlines we’re seeing in Google Search are downright tame:

[![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/03/google-replace-headlines_cc4709.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/03/google-replace-headlines_cc4709.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0,0,100,100)

But these are just the first headlines we’ve seen Google change. They may be the canary in the coal mine. Google may alter the deal even further.

While Google says this is an “experiment,” you shouldn’t assume that means the company won’t roll it out more widely, because Google originally told us its AI headlines in Google Discover were an experiment too. A month later, it told us those AI headlines are now a feature, one that “performs well for user satisfaction.”

[![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/03/chrome_5pIQWgxvN4.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/03/chrome_5pIQWgxvN4.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0,0,100,100)

*[The actual story](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/654223/cheat-on-everything-ai) that Google Search boiled down to “‘Cheat on everything’ AI tool.”*

[![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/03/chrome_WSBurulWgj.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/03/chrome_WSBurulWgj.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0,0,100,100)

*[The actual story](https://www.theverge.com/2024/8/22/24225997/microsoft-copilot-rebrand-changes) Google turned into “Copilot Changes: Marketing Teams at it Again.”*

Google did not explain why the company is no longer respecting the headline identifiers it has long encouraged newsrooms to use. The company did answer some specific questions via email, though.

Google told us that the overall idea is to “identify content on a page that would be a useful and relevant title to a users’ query.” The goal is “better matching titles to users’ queries and facilitating engagement with web content,” according to Kutz.

This test is “not specific to news publications, but looking at how we can improve titles horizontally,” according to Adriance. Google confirmed that the test uses generative AI, but claimed that “if we were to actually launch something based on this experiment, it would not be using a generative model and we would not be creating headlines with gen AI,” according to De Leon. Google did not explain how it might replace our story titles *without* generative AI.

Mostly, Google’s answers tried to normalize the idea of replacing headlines in search — suggesting that this is just one of [the “tens of thousands of live traffic experiments”](https://go.skimresources.com/?id=1025X1701640&xs=1&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.google.com%2Fintl%2Fen_us%2Fsearch%2Fhowsearchworks%2Fhow-search-works%2Frigorous-testing%2F) that Google runs to test possible improvements to Google Search, and reminding us that it’s [already been tweaking the titles of webpages in Search to help users](https://developers.google.com/search/blog/2021/09/more-info-about-titles) for many years now.

But I want to be clear: **This is not normal.** I’ve edited tech news for 15 years, paying close attention to SEO, and I’ve never before seen Google overwrite a headline in search results with something it created itself.

The changes that Google typically makes to a news story’s title are far simpler. If Google’s algorithms decide a headline is too long or lopsided, it’ll sometimes show you only part of that headline, lopping off the beginning or end. Here are two recent examples of that:

[![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/03/SCR-20260318-lcdz.png?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/03/SCR-20260318-lcdz.png?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0,0,100,100)

[![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/03/SCR-20260318-jghi.png?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0%2C0%2C100%2C100&w=2400)](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/03/SCR-20260318-jghi.png?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0,0,100,100)

Or, if a story has two headlines, one that we flag as the “search headline” and one that we flag as the “on-page headline,” Google will sometimes display the on-page headline instead of the one we crafted for a more general search audience. (We currently set those headlines inside WordPress, the popular content management platform behind many leading websites, but I’ve used those fields inside other backends too.) This tendency of Google Search has been annoying over the years, but nowhere near as annoying as an AI creating “Copilot Changes: Marketing Teams at it Again” out of whole cloth.

Changing headlines, and their meaning, makes journalism less trustworthy at a time when powerful institutions are trying to discredit it, *and* when many news organizations are struggling just to keep the lights on.

[We’ve](https://www.theverge.com/2023/5/12/23720396/google-search-generative-experience-blue-links) [warned](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/631352/ai-search-adobe-analytics-google-perplexity-openai) [for years](https://www.theverge.com/2023/5/10/23717120/google-search-ai-results-generated-experience-io) that Google is prioritizing AI search over the “10 blue links,” and I am frequently frustrated that its Gemini AI search doesn’t encourage clicking through to actual news sources. But I figured that I could always [fall back](https://www.theverge.com/2024/5/14/24074314/google-now-offers-web-search) to those blue links to get a relatively unadulterated experience. Now, I have to wonder.

**Follow topics and authors** from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

- Sean Hollister

highlights.title: Quiche Browser
highlights.summary:
# Quiche Browser Summary

Quiche Browser is an independent, privacy-focused web browser for iOS that has garnered significant acclaim for its exceptional customization and minimalist design. Built by a passionate indie developer, it offers users unprecedented control over their browsing experience, allowing them to customize every button and toolbar element to suit their preferences. The browser combines thoughtful design with practical features, including a built-in ad blocker, system-wide dark mode, and zero usage monitoring to protect user privacy.

Despite its extensive customization options, Quiche Browser maintains an intuitive and elegant interface that reviewers have praised for feeling intentional rather than cluttered. The app has achieved remarkable success with over 50,000 downloads and a 4.9-star average rating from more than 1,300 reviews. Major tech publications including The Verge, MacStories, 9to5Mac, and Lifehacker have highlighted it as an excellent alternative to Safari for users seeking a lightweight, private, and fully tailored browsing experience.
highlights.content:
## Beautifully customizable.

        An independent, private, and transparent browser built by a passionate maker. Thoughtfully designed customization options and quality-of-life improvements without sacrificing ease of use. Established browsers can’t compare.

        

      

    

    
      
        - 🎨Unmatched customization

        - 🌅Elegantly minimalist

        - 🛡️Built-in blocker

        - 🌙Dark mode everywhere

        - 🔒Zero usage monitoring

        - 🌱Independent, transparent

      

    

    
      
## Praised and loved.

      
        - 
          50,000+
          Down­loads
        

        - 
          1300+
          App Store ratings
        

        - 
          4.9★
          Average Rating (U.S.)
        

      

      
> 
> 
> [
> ![The Verge logo](https://quiche.industries/assets/theverge.svg)
> ](https://www.theverge.com/installer-newsletter/633860/pebble-2-duo-assassins-creed-shadows-pixel-9a-installer#screen-share)
> 
> 
> “My favorite iOS browser these days is Quiche Browser. It’s somehow both incredibly simple and one of the most customizable browsers I’ve ever tried, which is a really hard balance to pull off. […] It’s great.”

      
> 
> 
> [
> ![MacStories logo](https://quiche.industries/assets/macstories.svg)
> ](https://www.macstories.net/reviews/quiche-browser-is-a-beautiful-and-modular-web-browser-for-ios/)
> 
> 
> “Quiche Browser has clearly been designed with care. Despite its commitment to modularity and customization, Quiche Browser’s UI still feels intentional.”

      
> 
> 
> [
> ![9to5Mac logo](https://quiche.industries/assets/9to5mac.svg)
> ](https://9to5mac.com/2025/10/11/indie-app-spotlight-quiche-customizable-iphone-web-browser/)
> 
> 
> “If you want a lightweight, private, minimalistic, yet customizable web browsing experience on your iPhone – [Quiche Browser] might be the perfect answer for you. It also offers a number of unique features to make it more tailored for power users than Safari.”

      
> 
> 
> [
> ![Lifehacker logo](https://quiche.industries/assets/lifehacker.svg)
> ](https://lifehacker.com/tech/custom-iphone-browser-quiche)
> 
> 
> “Quiche Browser is unique, engaging, and fully customizable, down to every button and toolbar you see in the interface. […] [It] has some excellent ideas that other browsers should take note of.”

    

    
      
## Make it yours. Control freaks welcome.

      
        - 
          
### Buttons where you need them

          Choose and place every button in your toolbar to suit your needs and arrangement preferences. Why settle for the same one-size-fits-all browser as everyone else?

          
            
              
              ![](https://quiche.industries/browser/assets/home/toolbars.png)
            
          
        

        - 
          
### You make the menu

          Place less-used buttons in a popover menu, keeping essential tools within reach without cluttering your toolbar. Open the menu however you prefer: using a dedicated button, a single tap on the address bar, or a long press.

          
            
              
              
            
          
        

        - 
          
### Get your tabs in order

          Choose between a list or grid layout, adjust snapshots to be large or small, sort by recency or read time, and group by website whenever you want to read all open pages from the same site in one go.
          
            
              
              ![](https://quiche.industries/browser/assets/home/tabs.png)
            
          
        

      

      
> ★★★★★ V,M, App Store US
> “Customising the menus is a feature that I never knew I needed — but now I’ve got them set up how I like them, I can never go back.”

      
> ★★★★★ ONEobservant, App Store US
> “This browser is actually PURE awesomeness. It has the most easily customizable features I'd ever seen to date in a browser.”

    

    
      
## As beautiful as the Web, just less messy.

      
        - 
          
### Non-boring address bars

          Pick a visual style and choose which page info you want to see: domain or full address, title, favicon, or read time.

          
            
              
              ![](https://quiche.industries/browser/assets/home/location.png)
            
          
        

        - 
          
### Custom colors for your custom browser

          Select from various background colors or set it to automatically match the site’s color. Choose different colors for light and dark mode.

          
            
              
              ![](https://quiche.industries/browser/assets/home/colors.png)
            
          
        

        - 
          
### Go hardcore-minimal

          Move some of your buttons into a popover menu that can appear when you tap the address bar or a dedicated menu button, letting websites take the spotlight. You can even remove the address bar altogether.

          
            
              
              ![](https://quiche.industries/browser/assets/home/minimal.png)
            
          
        

      

      
> ★★★★★ Luhmann, App Store US
> “I think it gets the balance between minimalism and customizability just right.”

      
> ★★★★★ Yushipoo, App Store US
> “A minimalists dream. An incredibly creative and well crafted browser with tons of potential from a developer who cares.”

      
> ★★★★★ James_SA, App Store UK
> “The design of this app is top-notch, rare for a browser this customisable!”

    

    
      
## Convenience features you didn’t know you needed.

      
        - 
          
### Quiche Blocker

          Ads, trackers, cookie banners, and other insufferable nuisances are all blocked by default.
        

        - 
          
### Website Darkening

          Dark mode for all websites.
        

        - 
          
### Support any search engine

          Even Kagi.
        

        - 
          
### Quick actions in your toolbar

          Add buttons for closing all tabs and deleting data, moving tabs to private mode, loading the current page in Google Translate, disabling JavaScript, and more.
        

        - 
          
### Customizable scrolling behavior

          Choose to condense or hide the toolbar completely as you scroll.
        

        - 
          
### Extreme energy savings

          Automatically suspend all background tabs when Low Power Mode is turned on on your device.
        

      

    

    
      
## Keep your data for yourself.

      
        - 
          
### No sign-up, obviously

          Since when did it become normal to require an account to use a web browser?
        

        - 
          
### Zero usage monitoring

          No usage monitoring or telemetry. I prefer talking directly with users rather than spying on numbers.
        

        - 
          
### Never phones home, doesn't even have one

          Quiche Browser doesn’t own any backend server or connect to third-party services, with the exception of [RevenueCat](https://www.revenuecat.com/) to manage purchases and prevent fraud. Verify this yourself by inspecting network traffic through a proxy.

        

        - 
          
### Optional search suggestions

          You can turn off search engine suggestions in private tabs, or everywhere.

        

      

      [Read the privacy policy](https://quiche.industries/browser/privacy)

    

    
      
## Lightweight, fast, and original.

      Most browsers on the App Store are just bloated clones of Chrome, Brave, or Firefox, weighed down by years of technical and design debt. On the other hand, Quiche Browser was built entirely from scratch.

      A bit crazy ambitious for a one-person project, but this lean foundation makes it easier to build upon, lowers memory usage, and ensures faster app downloads and updates.

    

    
      
## Independent and here to stay.

      I initially built Quiche Browser for myself, out of frustration with the rigidity and conservatism of most web browsers.

      As an independent app, all product decisions come directly from me, a full-time user. This freedom is a huge advantage over browsers tied to unsustainable financial deals or startups controlled by investors pushing for unrealistic growth and billion-dollar returns, almost always leading to [enshittification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enshittification).

      That’s why Quiche Browser will stay niche, laser-focused, and financially sustainable. By keeping expenses minimal, it’s designed to never go bankrupt.

      [Read more about me and my principles](https://quiche.industries/)

    

    
      
## User funded.

      My goal for Quiche Browser is to grow it enough to cover my living expenses so I can focus on it full-time and step away from side jobs.

      If you’d like to show your support, help Quiche Browser grow faster, and see it eventually ported to Mac, you can send tips in-app or subscribe to **Quiche PLUS**, a completely optional subscription that unlocks website darkening, all app icons, button customizations, and my eternal gratitude 🫶

> “Love at first sight, excellent dev support, great roadmap, friendly monetization.”

      
> ★★★★★ turbotadventure, App Store US
> “Quiche is delicious in real life and the features of this browser are also the utmost decadent. I believe a solo developer made it, and they are the embodiment of a thousand loving grandmother energy.”

      
> ★★★★★ joshtransient, App Store US
> “It's become my default browser. So much love and care from the dev.”

> “What a great configurable browser! Greg develops and supports it, you get quick answers to all your requests. Where else can you find this?”

      
> ★★★★★ Luke//codex, App Store US
> “Hands down best browser on iOS. Actually AMAZING. Change literally everything. I can tell that the developer really does care about what they are making, and that makes me happy.”

      
> ★★★★★ luemmelfitz, App Store Germany
